'''''Camellia oleifera''''', which originated in China, is notable as an important source of edible oil (known as [[tea oil]] or camellia oil) obtained from its seeds.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.huntingtonbotanical.org/Camellia/collections.htm|title=The Huntington Botanical Gardens: The Camellia Garden|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140224033512/http://www.huntingtonbotanical.org/Camellia/collections.htm|archive-date=2014-02-24}}</ref> It is commonly known as the '''oil-seed camellia''' or '''tea oil camellia''', though to a lesser extent other species of ''[[camellia]]'' are used in oil production too.

It is widely distributed in China and is cultivated extensively there. It is found in [[forest]]s, thickets, banks of streams and foothills at elevations of 500 to 1,300 metres.<ref name="Plants for a future">{{Cite web |url=http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Camellia+oleifera |title=Plants for a Future |access-date=2015-01-16 |archive-date=2016-03-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303212328/http://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Camellia+oleifera |url-status=live }}</ref>

This species looks much similar to ''[[Camellia sasanqua]]'' except the dark green, evergreen leaves are a bit larger, three to five inches long and two to three inches wide. Single, white, fragrant flowers are produced in mid to late fall, and this large shrub or small tree will reach a height of 20 feet with thin, upright, multiple trunks and branches.
The crown forms a rounded or oval vase with lower branches removed.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://hort.ufl.edu/trees/CAMOLEA.pdf|via=[[University of Florida]]|publisher=[[USDA]] [[United States Forest Service|Forest Service]] |last1=Gilman|first1=Edward F. |last2=Watson|first2=Dennis G.|title=Fact Sheet ST-116 Camellia oleifera Tea-Oil Camellia|date=November 1993|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160531193747/http://hort.ufl.edu/trees/CAMOLEA.pdf|archive-date=May 31, 2016 }}</ref>

==Uses==
{{Main|Tea seed oil}}
The seeds of ''Camellia oleifera'' can be pressed to yield [[tea seed oil]], a sweetish seasoning and cooking oil. In tea seed oil, [[oleic acid]], a monounsaturated fatty acid comprises ~80% of the total fatty acid content - the oil is similar in composition to [[olive oil]]. After the tea seed oil is extracted, the seed itself still serves a purpose. The ''Camellia'' oil cake is used as an anti-inflammatory and antioxidant.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Xiao |first=Xiaomei |last2=He |first2=Liangmei |last3=Chen |first3=Yayun |last4=Wu |first4=Longhuo |last5=Wang |first5=Lin |last6=Liu |first6=Zhiping |date=November 2017 |title=Anti-inflammatory and antioxidative effects of Camellia oleifera Abel components |url=https://www.future-science.com/doi/10.4155/fmc-2017-0109 |journal=Future Medicinal Chemistry |volume=9 |issue=17 |pages=2069–2079 |doi=10.4155/fmc-2017-0109 |issn=1756-8919|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Tea oil is also known as "tea seed oil" when sold as cooking oil in supermarkets throughout Australia, New Zealand and the United States.<ref name="Antioxidant Activity and Bioactive Compounds of Tea Seed Oil">{{cite journal|journal=[[Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry]]|volume=54|issue=3|pages=779–784|doi=10.1021/jf052325a|last1=Lee|first1=Chia-Pu |last2=Yen|first2=Gow-Chin|location=Taiwan|title=Antioxidant Activity and Bioactive Compounds of Tea Seed (''Camellia oleifera'' Abel.) Oil}}</ref>

It can also be used in textile manufacture, in [[soap making]] and, when burned in an [[oil lamp]], as a source of light.<ref name="Plants for a future"/> ''Camellia'' oil is also traditionally used to protect Japanese woodworking tools and cutlery from corrosion and is currently sold for that purpose.<ref>Odate, T: "Japanese Woodworking Tools: Their Tradition, Spirit, and Use" page 174. Linden Publishing, Reprint edition 1998.</ref><ref>Nakahara, Y; Sato, H.; Nii, P.: "Complete Japanese Joinery: A Handbook of Japanese Tool Use and Woodworking for Joiners and Carpenters" pages 5, 15, 28.  Hartley & Marks Publishers, 1998</ref>

==See also==
* [[Tea tree oil]] is derived from ''[[Melaleuca alternifolia]]'' -  it is an essential oil used for medical and cosmetic purposes and is toxic when ingested.
* [[Leptospermum|Tea tree]] is a name sometimes applied to a number of different species of plants endemic to Australia. These plants are unrelated to the [[tea plant]].
